name.text: WAT 04.1: No Such Thing as a Char!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four functions that read characters out of a string, count them, and return a relabelled copy.

How this works in Python

Java reaches into a string with charAt, asks how long it is with the length() method, and hands you back a char, which is a primitive type all of its own.

String code = "north-pier";
char first = code.charAt(0);
char last  = code.charAt(code.length() - 1);
int size   = code.length();

Python does all three differently, and the last of them is the one that saves you an off-by-one error for the rest of your career.

Indexing

Python uses square brackets, the same brackets Java uses on an array. code[0] is the first character and counting starts at zero, exactly as in Java.

There is no char

code[0] gives you back a string one character long. Python has no separate character type, so a single letter and a whole paragraph are both the type str. Nothing needs converting between the two.

Negative indexing

A negative index counts from the right hand end. code[-1] is the last character and code[-2] is the one before it. Read -1 as "one from the end". Writing code[len(code) - 1] works and marks you out as someone still thinking in Java.

code = "north-pier"
print(code[0])    # n
print(code[-1])   # r

Length is a function, not a method

You ask with len(code). There is no .length() and no .length attribute. The same len works on anything that has a size, which is why it sits outside the string rather than on it.

Methods come back new

Python strings are immutable, exactly as Java strings are, so an assignment such as code[0] = "X" raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. Every string method leaves the original alone and returns a fresh string, so a method call whose result you throw away is a call you have wasted. Two of them do the work below.

  • text.upper() returns an upper-case copy. It is Java's toUpperCase.
  • text.replace(old, new) returns a copy with every occurrence of old swapped for new. Unlike Java's version it takes plain text, not a regular expression.

Method calls chain left to right, so code.replace("-", "/").upper() replaces first and upper-cases the result.

Your task

Write four functions. Each one returns a value. None of them prints.

  • first_letter(text) returns the first character of text.
  • last_letter(text) returns the last character of text, reached from the right hand end.
  • letter_count(text) returns how many characters text holds.
  • relabel(code) swaps every hyphen for a slash and returns the result in upper case, so "north-pier" becomes "NORTH/PIER". The caller's string comes back untouched, because you cannot touch it.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Reach the last character with a negative index. text[len(text) - 1] is banned.
  • Ask for the length with len(text). There is no .length and no .length().
  • Do not write charAt. It does not exist here.
  • No loops. One chained method call relabels the whole string.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (first_letter, last_letter, letter_count, relabel)) assert ".length" not in whole, "rule broken: ask with len(text)" assert "charAt" not in whole, "rule broken: Python has no charAt" assert "[len(" not in whole, "rule broken: reach the last character with -1" assert "for " not in whole, "rule broken: no loops, one chained call does it" print(first_letter("x")) print(last_letter("x")) print(letter_count("")) print(relabel("a-b-c")) print(relabel("NORTH"))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three functions that each build one line of text with a single f-string.

How this works in Python

Java builds a line of text by gluing pieces together with +, and reaches for String.format when the glue gets unreadable.

String line  = name + " logged " + count + " readings";
String other = String.format("Station %s is online", name.toUpperCase());

The first line works because the Java compiler quietly converts count to text on your behalf. Python refuses to do that.

name = "Kaitaia"
count = 42
print(name + " logged " + count)
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

The Java reflex is to wrap the number in str(count). That runs, and it is the wrong answer. Python has one piece of syntax that replaces both of the Java lines above.

An f-string is an ordinary string literal with the letter f written in front of the opening quote. Inside an f-string, every pair of curly braces holds an expression. Python works out the expression, turns the result into text, and drops it into the line. Dropping a value into text this way is called interpolation. Java has nothing like it.

print(f"{name} logged {count} readings")   # Kaitaia logged 42 readings

Nothing is converted by hand, and the shape of the finished line is visible in the source instead of being hidden behind a row of plus signs.

Anything you can write as an expression goes between the braces, a method call included.

print(f"Station {name.upper()} is online")   # Station KAITAIA is online

Two details catch people out.

  • A single brace opens an interpolation, so a brace you want in the output has to be doubled. {{ produces one { and }} produces one }. Text that carries braces of its own, such as JSON, needs the doubled form.
  • The quotes around the f-string cannot be the same quotes you use inside it. When the text itself contains double quotes, wrap the whole f-string in single quotes.

Both details land at once in f'{{"{key}": {value}}}'. Read it left to right. f' opens the f-string, {{ is a literal opening brace, the double quote is literal text, {key} interpolates, the next double quote is literal, {value} interpolates, }} is a literal closing brace, and ' closes the f-string.

Field widths, decimal places and thousands separators also live inside the braces. They come later in this topic. Everything here is plain interpolation.

Your task

Write three functions. Each one returns a string. None of them prints.

  • receipt(name, count) returns Kaitaia logged 42 readings for the arguments ("Kaitaia", 42). The count is a whole number and no conversion happens.
  • shout_line(name) returns Station KAITAIA is online for "kaitaia". Upper-case it inside the braces.
  • as_json(key, value) returns {"site": 42} for ("site", 42). The key is wrapped in double quotes and the value, being a number, is not. The outer braces are part of the output.

A count of zero and a negative value are both ordinary values, so the same f-string handles them.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character, spaces included.

Rules
  • Build every returned line with one f-string. No +, no str(), no % formatting, no .format().
  • One string literal per function. Do not call join.
  • Build no text with +=.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

expected.text: Kaitaia logged 42 readings Otautahi logged 0 readings

testcode.text: import inspect sources = [inspect.getsource(f) for f in (receipt, shout_line, as_json)] whole = "".join(sources) assert "+" not in whole, "rule broken: no + concatenation" assert "str(" not in whole, "rule broken: no str()" assert ".format(" not in whole, "rule broken: no .format()" assert "%" not in whole, "rule broken: no % formatting" assert ".join(" not in whole, "rule broken: one f-string per function" assert "+=" not in whole, "rule broken: no += text building" for source in sources: assert 'f"' in source or "f'" in source, "rule broken: every line comes from an f-string" print(receipt("A", 1)) print(shout_line("te anau")) print(as_json("count", -7)) print(as_json("ratio", 0.5))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five functions that format numbers with f-string format specs and reshape text with string methods.

How this works in Python

Java builds text in four different ways. You join pieces with +. You call String.format when a field needs a fixed width. You reach for DecimalFormat when a number needs comma separators. You switch to StringBuilder when the joining happens inside a long loop.

String line = name + " (" + count + ")";
String padded = String.format("%-12s %,d", name, count);

Python replaces all four with one piece of syntax. An f-string is a string literal with the letter f written in front of the opening quote. Inside an f-string, Python reads whatever sits between a pair of curly braces, works out its value, and puts that value into the text. Dropping a value into text this way is called interpolation. Java has nothing like it.

name = "Kaitaia"
count = 42
print(f"{name} ({count})")     # Kaitaia (42)

Add a colon inside the braces and everything after that colon is a format spec. The format spec is a small language of its own. It controls the width of the field, the alignment inside that field, the number of decimal places, and the way a number is written. It does the work that String.format and DecimalFormat do in Java. This exercise uses four format specs.

Two more f-string features help you while you debug. Write an equals sign immediately before the closing brace, as in {reading=}, and Python prints the text reading= and then the value. Write !r immediately before the closing brace and Python prints the repr of the value. The repr of a value is the text you would type to recreate that value, so a string keeps its quotes. Under !r the number 4.5 prints as 4.5 and the string "4.5" prints as '4.5'. The two stop looking identical.

Python strings are immutable, exactly as Java strings are. Every method returns a new string and leaves the original untouched. You call a string method with a dot, the same way you do in Java. Four of those methods do the work in part two.

  • text.strip() with no argument removes the whitespace from both ends. It is Java's trim.
  • text.lower() returns a lower-case copy.
  • text.split() with no argument breaks the text apart wherever whitespace appears and returns a list of the words.
  • "-".join(words) glues a list of strings into one string and puts a - between each neighbouring pair. The separator sits on the left of the dot and the list goes inside the brackets. Read that aloud as "the hyphen joins these words" and the order stops looking backwards.

One method looks familiar and behaves differently. Java's replace(".txt", "") removes a whole piece of text, so Python's strip(".txt") looks like the same tool. It is not. Given an argument, strip reads that argument as a set of single characters and removes any of those characters from both ends. "Annual Report.txt".strip(".txt") returns "Annual Repor", because the final t of Report is in the set and goes as well. Use removesuffix(".txt") instead. It removes the whole suffix, once, and only from the end.

Your task

Write five functions. Each one returns a string. None of them prints.

  • calibration_line(site, count, ratio, code) returns one line built from these four format specs, in that order, with a | between them. For the arguments ("Kaitaia", 1234567, 0.8642, 15) it returns Kaitaia     |1,234,567|  86.4%|0x0f.
    • {site:<12} writes site in a field twelve characters wide and pushes it to the left. Spaces fill the rest of the field.
    • {count:>9,} writes count in a field nine characters wide and pushes it to the right. The comma groups the thousands, so 1234567 comes out as 1,234,567.
    • {ratio:>7.1%} multiplies ratio by 100 and writes one digit after the decimal point. It adds a percent sign, then pushes the result to the right in a field seven characters wide.
    • {code:#04x} writes code as lower-case hexadecimal. The # adds the 0x prefix. The 04 pads with leading zeros until the whole thing is four characters long, so 15 comes out as 0x0f.
  • debug_line(reading) uses the = debug form. For the value 4.5 it returns reading=4.5.
  • repr_line(reading) uses !r. For the string "4.5" it returns raw value '4.5'.
  • slugify(filename) turns " Annual Report.txt " into "annual-report". Strip both ends, remove the suffix, lower the case, split into words, then join the words with -.
  • tag_line(tags) joins a list of tags into one string and puts ", " between each neighbouring pair.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character, spaces included.

Rules
  • Build every returned line with one f-string. No +, no str(), no % formatting, no .format().
  • Pad and round inside the braces. ljust(), rjust() and round() are banned.
  • Do not use strip(".txt") to drop the extension. It strips characters, not a suffix, and a method named for exactly this job already exists.
  • Build no string with += in a loop. One call to join per result.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: reading = 4.5 print(debug_line(reading)) print(repr_line("4.5")) print(repr_line(4.5)) print(slugify(" Annual Report.txt ")) print(slugify("QUARTERLY Sensor Log.txt")) print(tag_line(["radar", "north", "calibrated"])) print(tag_line(["solo"]))

expected.text: reading=4.5 raw value '4.5' raw value 4.5 annual-report quarterly-sensor-log radar, north, calibrated solo

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (calibration_line, debug_line, repr_line, slugify, tag_line)) assert "+" not in whole, "rule broken: no + concatenation" assert "str(" not in whole, "rule broken: no str()" assert ".format(" not in whole, "rule broken: no .format()" assert ".ljust(" not in whole and ".rjust(" not in whole, "rule broken: pad inside the braces" assert "round(" not in whole, "rule broken: round inside the braces" assert "removesuffix(" in inspect.getsource(slugify), "rule broken: use removesuffix" assert 'strip(".txt")' not in whole and "strip('.txt')" not in whole, "rule broken: strip eats characters" assert "+=" not in whole, "rule broken: no += string building" print(calibration_line("Te Anau", 0, 0.0, 0)) print(slugify("report.txt.txt")) print(repr_line(tag_line([])))
